```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
```

limn turns a model fitted by [illume](https://github.com/huttoncp/illume) into
predictive distributions: for a unit in the data or a new one, for the next
weeks of a series, or for totals over many of them. It scores those
distributions against what happened, checks their calibration, and compares
models with standard errors that respect how the data hang together. When one
of its checks finds something wrong, it says what it found, why that matters,
and what to do about it.

This vignette walks through one small example from start to finish: fit,
predict, forecast, total, score, check, remedy and compare.

```{r setup}
library(limn)
```

## The data and a first model

Twenty clinics report their weekly number of visits for 36 weeks. A clinic's
count depends on its size and on the temperature, and clinics differ: some are
busier than their size says. The simulation draws the counts from a negative
binomial distribution, so they vary more than Poisson counts with the same
mean would.

```{r data}
set.seed(1001)
n_clinics <- 20; n_weeks <- 36
clinics <- data.frame(clinic = factor(sprintf("C%02d", 1:n_clinics)),
                      size = round(runif(n_clinics, 0.5, 2), 1))
visits <- expand.grid(week = 1:n_weeks, clinic = clinics$clinic)
visits$size <- clinics$size[visits$clinic]
visits$temp <- round(10 + 8 * sin(2 * pi * visits$week / 52) + rnorm(nrow(visits)), 1)
clinic_effect <- rnorm(n_clinics, 0, 0.3)
mu <- exp(1.6 + 0.5 * log(visits$size) - 0.03 * visits$temp + clinic_effect[visits$clinic])
visits$count <- rnbinom(nrow(visits), size = 3, mu = mu)
train <- visits[visits$week <= 30, ]
test <- visits[visits$week > 30, ]
```

The last six weeks are held back to check the forecasts. The first model,
fitted by illume, is a Poisson regression with a random intercept for each
clinic. It is a reasonable first guess, and a wrong one: the checks below find
out.

```{r fit}
fit <- illume::ilm_model(count ~ log(size) + temp + (1 | clinic), data = train,
                         family = "poisson", verbose = FALSE)
```

## Predictions: which unit?

A mixed model predicts different things for the same row, depending on the
question: this clinic, a new clinic, a typical one, or the average over
clinics. So `ilm_predict()` asks. Here `groups = "fitted"` predicts each row's
own clinic. A clinic the fit has not seen is predicted as a new one, with its
effect drawn from the fitted distribution of clinics, and is marked as such:

```{r predict}
nd <- data.frame(clinic = c("C01", "new"), size = 1, temp = 10, week = 31)
p <- ilm_predict(fit, nd, groups = "fitted", nsim = 500)
as.data.frame(p)
```

These are predictions of the mean count. For clinic C01, `estimate` is the
mean at the fitted parameters; for the new clinic, whose effect is unknown, it
is the predictive median. `mean` averages over everything the prediction is
uncertain about, and the limits are those of the central 90% interval. The new
clinic's interval is wider: it carries the uncertainty in its own effect.

The other choices are `groups = "new"`, `"typical"` (the effects at zero) and
`"population"` (the average over clinics). By default every parameter is drawn
jointly, the variances included (`uncertainty = "joint"`); see `?ilm_predict`
for the other choices.

## Forecasts

`ilm_future()` builds the rows a forecast needs: the next weeks of every
clinic. It copies what does not change over time, such as a clinic's size, and
leaves what does, the temperature, for you to fill in:

```{r future}
fut <- ilm_future(train, time = "week", group = "clinic", h = 6, response = "count")
head(fut, 3)
```

Here the temperatures are taken from the held-back weeks. That makes this an
*ex-post* forecast, one "made using later information on the predictors"
(fpp3, section 7.6). A forecast made at week 30 would not know them, and
would mix over plausible temperature paths instead: `ilm_covariate_paths()`
draws them from a model of the temperature, and `ilm_as_draws()` takes them
from another tool.

```{r forecast}
fut$temp <- test$temp[match(paste(fut$clinic, fut$week), paste(test$clinic, test$week))]
fc <- ilm_forecast(fit, fut, nsim = 500)
head(as.data.frame(fc), 4)
```

A forecast is the distribution of a new count, so `estimate` is now its median
and `mean` its expected value. This model has no correlation over time, so a
clinic's forecast depends only on its effect, its size and the week's
temperature. With one, such as `illume::ilm_ar1()`, each clinic's recent run
of busy or quiet weeks would carry forward too; see `?ilm_forecast`.

## Totals

The total over clinics is not the sum of their intervals. `ilm_aggregate()`
sums the forecasts draw by draw, so what the clinics share, the model's
parameters, carries into the total:

```{r aggregate}
total <- ilm_aggregate(fc, by = "week")
as.data.frame(total)
```

A fan chart shows the weekly total with the observed totals before it:

```{r fan}
observed <- aggregate(count ~ week, data = train, FUN = sum)
ilm_plot_fan(total, time = "week", history = observed, response = "count")
```

The line is the forecast total's median, and the bands are its central 50%,
80% and 95% intervals, after the observed totals of the first 30 weeks.

## Checking the forecasts

With the held-back weeks, the forecasts can be scored. `ilm_scores()` gives one
score per row for each rule asked for: here the log score, the continuous
ranked probability score (CRPS) and the interval score of the central 90%
interval (Gneiting and Raftery 2007, sections 4.1, 4.2 and 6.2). Each is a
loss: lower is better.

```{r scores}
s <- ilm_scores(fc, test$count, rules = c("log", "crps", "interval"))
colMeans(s[attr(s, "rules")])
```

A score means most beside another model's. On its own, the first question is
whether outcomes fell where the forecasts said they would. `ilm_calibration()`
checks the coverage of central intervals level by level, the bias of the mean,
and the uniformity of the probability integral transforms (PITs), and ends
with a verdict:

```{r calibration}
cal <- ilm_calibration(fc, test$count)
cal
```

The intervals are far too narrow, at every level. The verdict names the usual
cause for counts, and the remedy: a family whose variance can exceed its mean.
The PIT histogram shows the same:

```{r pit}
ilm_plot_pit(ilm_pit(fc, test$count))
```

If the forecasts are right, the PITs are uniform, and each bar falls inside
the shaded band with probability 0.95; with ten bars, one may stray outside
it by chance. This histogram is far from flat. The bar nearest 0 is nearly
three times as high as it should be and the middle bars are low: too many
outcomes fell in the tails of their predictive distributions, and nearly all
of the excess is in the lower tail. Gneiting, Balabdaoui and Raftery (2007,
section 3.1, p. 253) note that "U-shaped histograms often correspond to
predictive distributions that are too narrow". A histogram that slopes one way
can also mean bias (see `?ilm_plot_pit`), but the calibration check found no
bias in the mean beyond sampling error.

The fit's own checks in illume found nothing to remedy:

```{r remedies}
illume::ilm_remedies(fit)
```

The problem shows only when the forecasts meet new data, which is what limn
checks. The check treats the 120 held-back outcomes as independent, though
they share clinics and weeks, so its standard errors may be too small. Here
the shortfall is large at every level.

## The remedy, and the check again

The remedy is a change to the model, so it is made in illume: refit with a
negative binomial family, forecast the same rows, and check again.

```{r remedy}
fit_nb <- illume::ilm_model(count ~ log(size) + temp + (1 | clinic), data = train,
                            family = "nbinom", verbose = FALSE)
fc_nb <- ilm_forecast(fit_nb, fut, nsim = 500)
ilm_calibration(fc_nb, test$count)
ilm_plot_pit(ilm_pit(fc_nb, test$count))
```

The intervals now cover about as often as they should, and every bar of the
PIT histogram is within the band.

## Comparing the two models

Scores compare the two models. Both are scored on the same rows, and
`ilm_compare()` tests the difference. The rows share clinics, so the standard
error is clustered by clinic:
<!-- awaiting the primary source for the cluster-robust standard error:
Cameron and Miller (2015) or Liang and Zeger (1986); cite it at a page once
read -->

```{r compare}
s_nb <- ilm_scores(fc_nb, test$count, rules = c("log", "crps", "interval"))
ilm_compare(poisson = cbind(test["clinic"], s["log"]),
            nbinom = cbind(test["clinic"], s_nb["log"]), rule = "log", by = "clinic")
```

The negative binomial model's log score is lower by about five standard
errors, though its intervals are wider.

## Cross-validation over rolling origins

One held-back stretch is one test. Rolling origins give several: at each origin
the model is refitted to the weeks up to it and forecasts the weeks after it,
which fpp3 (section 5.10) calls "evaluation on a rolling forecasting origin".
`ilm_folds()` builds the origins, here every week from week 20 to week 33,
each forecasting three weeks ahead. `ilm_cv()` refits and scores each one:

```{r cv}
folds <- ilm_folds(visits, type = "rolling", time = "week", group = "clinic",
                   initial = 20, horizon = 3, step = 1)
cv <- ilm_cv(fit, visits, folds, rules = "log", nsim = 200)
cv
```

`ilm_cv()` flags that the evaluation is *ex-post*: each fold's forecast rows
carry the temperature that was observed, which would not be known at the
origin. If a covariate's future values would be known, such as a calendar
effect, name it in `ilm_folds(known = )`, and the evaluation is *ex-ante*.

The same folds score the negative binomial model, and `ilm_compare()` tests
the difference origin by origin:

```{r cv-compare}
cv_nb <- ilm_cv(fit_nb, visits, folds, rules = "log", nsim = 200)
ilm_compare(poisson = cv, nbinom = cv_nb, by = "origin")
```

The negative binomial model's log score is lower pooled over the horizons and
at each horizon, every p-value below 0.02. Forecasts from neighbouring origins
overlap, so the origin means are correlated, and the test allows for it. It is
the fixed-m test of Coroneo and Iacone (2020, section 4.2), one of their
fixed-smoothing tests. In limn's own simulation it held its size from 10
origins up, which is why this example has 14 (see `?ilm_compare`).

## References

Coroneo, L. and Iacone, F. (2020). Comparing predictive accuracy in small
samples using fixed-smoothing asymptotics. *Journal of Applied Econometrics*
35(4), 391-409. Section 4.2.

Gneiting, T., Balabdaoui, F. and Raftery, A. E. (2007). Probabilistic
forecasts, calibration and sharpness. *Journal of the Royal Statistical
Society B* 69, 243-268. Section 3.1, p. 253.

Gneiting, T. and Raftery, A. E. (2007). Strictly proper scoring rules,
prediction, and estimation. *Journal of the American Statistical Association*
102(477), 359-378. Sections 4.1, 4.2 and 6.2.

Hyndman, R. J. and Athanasopoulos, G. (2021). *Forecasting: Principles and
Practice*, 3rd edition. OTexts. Section 5.10, "Time series cross-validation",
and section 7.6, "Forecasting with regression" (online edition,
<https://otexts.com/fpp3/>, read 19 October 2026).
